name: Capability Study, Part 3 — What Makes a Task Difficult (controlled, 60 tasks)
author: Omer
objective: Primary Goal: Parts 1-2 showed difficulty-3 tasks collapse to 18%, but difficulty and app-count are confounded in AppWorld's own labels — mean num_apps rises 1.18 / 1.55 / 2.47 across levels 1/2/3. This experiment asks whether task COMPLEXITY hurts on its own, separately from multi-app coordination.

Design: 20 tasks at each difficulty level, restricted to ground-truth num_apps == 1. Holding app-count constant means any remaining drop is caused by complexity alone — longer reference solutions and more API calls. Available single-app pool: 168 / 138 / 24 tasks at d1 / d2 / d3. Random sample, seed 20260720.

Instrumentation: beyond pass/fail, each task was measured for ReAct steps used versus plan steps written (does the agent finish its own plan?), API calls made versus the reference solution's num_api_calls (does it gather enough data?), and where it broke (near-miss versus wrong-from-start versus killed by the known retry bug).
environment: Branch: feat/specialists-and-success-rate, commit dfb58c7 (Gilad). Isolated git worktree.
Models: Executor / Explorer / Reviewer all gpt-4.1-mini | Temperature=0.1
Scoring: world.evaluate() — the official AppWorld scorer.
quantitative: Controlled results — app-count held at 1 across all three levels:
Effort comparison, solved versus failed tasks (steps used / API-call ratio against reference solution):
qualitative: [1] Complexity does hurt on its own — but multi-app breadth hurts far more.

With app-count held at 1 the curve is a gentle 85% / 70% / 50%. The unrestricted curve from Parts 1-2 was 62% / 57% / 18%. Single-app difficulty-3 scores 50% against 18% unrestricted, so most of what AppWorld's difficulty label captures is coordination cost, not complexity. Complexity alone costs roughly 35 points across three levels; adding apps costs far more. Single-app d1 likewise scores 85% against 62% unrestricted — a 23-point gap that is purely the confound.
[2] The agent does not give up: step coverage is about 0.90 at every level.

It consistently executes the plan it wrote for itself, and only one task in 60 exhausted the ReAct step budget. Plans also scale correctly with difficulty (5.8 / 9.0 / 9.2 steps). Neither planning discipline nor MAX_REACT_STEPS is the binding constraint.
[3] Failing tasks work harder, not less — the agent thrashes rather than quits.

At every level, failed tasks consume more ReAct steps than solved ones. At difficulty 2 they make roughly 2.5 times the API calls of the reference solution. This is unproductive searching, not under-exploration: the agent keeps fetching without converging. The one exception is difficulty 1, where the three failures under-called at 0.52 — short lookup tasks answered too early on too little data, which is the premature-submission mode identified in Part 1.
[4] From difficulty 2 upward, the retry bug becomes the dominant failure mode.

retry_killed accounts for 0 of 3 failures at d1, but 5 of 6 at d2 and 7 of 10 at d3 — 12 of the 16 failures above difficulty 1. The hardest tasks are exactly where the Reviewer fires most often, and exactly where its corrected output is discarded by the stale-completion race. The measured d2 and d3 rates therefore UNDERSTATE the pipeline's real capability: a large share of those failures are a plumbing defect, not a reasoning limit.
[5] Aggregate API volume at difficulty 3 is the one genuine under-exploration signal.

The reference solution needs 74 API calls; the agent averages 35. Across the d3 slice it gathers roughly half the data the task requires. Combined with finding [3], the picture is an agent that fetches the wrong things energetically rather than the right things insufficiently.
conclusions: Key insight: 'difficulty' is not one thing. Decomposed, it is mostly multi-app coordination cost, plus a smaller complexity cost — and above difficulty 1 the majority of remaining failures are the known retry bug rather than any reasoning limit.
[1] Fixing the retry path is worth more than Parts 1-2 suggested. It is concentrated precisely on the hard tasks, accounting for 12 of the 16 failures above difficulty 1.
[2] Multi-app coordination, not task complexity, is the dominant capability gap. Single-app d3 at 50% versus unrestricted d3 at 18% quantifies it directly.
[3] Do NOT raise MAX_REACT_STEPS. Only one task in 60 exhausted it, and failing tasks already use more steps than successful ones — more budget would extend the thrashing, not fix it.
[4] For hard single-app tasks the productive direction is convergence, not more searching: help the Executor recognise when it has gathered enough data rather than letting it keep querying.
Caveat: the d3 single-app pool contains only 24 tasks, so that cell is close to exhaustive rather than a wide random sample.
